results.method: Static IAM evaluation of the deployed control-plane policy and the bootstrap template, rendered for a sample tenant; each link checked with negative controls
results.summary: Every link of platform role → AssumeRole(ExternalId = tenant ID) → deployment role → s3:GetObject is allowed. The onboarding trust statement has no time bound, so the capability lasts as long as the bootstrap stack does.

results.claim: No secret is stored in plaintext; stored secrets are AES-256-GCM ciphertexts
results.method: Read-only queries: format, authentication under the current key and IV uniqueness of every stored ciphertext; erasure on deleted tenants; a credential-pattern scan of every text column of every table
results.summary: The accounts matches are operators' GitHub sign-in tokens, which the next-auth Drizzle adapter (src/auth.ts) stores as GitHub returns them. Nothing in the platform reads them after sign-in; it dispatches with GITHUB_PAT.
evidence: 2 stored ciphertexts across 16 tenants; malformed: 0
authenticate under PLATFORM_ENCRYPTION_KEY: 2/2
reused 96-bit IVs: 0 (GCM loses confidentiality and integrity if an IV repeats under one key)
deleted tenants still holding secrets: none
credential-pattern matches outside the encrypted columns: accounts.refresh_token github_token ×3; accounts.access_token github_token ×5 (850 cells scanned)

results.claim: No secret is recoverable from the public repository or its CI logs
results.method: gitleaks (default rules plus OpenRouter and Pinecone) over every commit and every retained Actions log, with reviewed false positives; exact search for every secret the operator holds
evidence: git history: 9 gitleaks findings, 9 reviewed as false positives (gitleaks-triage.json)
Actions logs: 116 runs, 67 with retained logs (134 files, 6.6 MB, oldest 2026-08-27T00:35:05Z), unavailable by HTTP status {"410":49}; 6 gitleaks findings
unreviewed findings: 0

known secrets searched: 8 (DEPLOY_WEBHOOK_SECRET, GITHUB_PAT, AUTH_SECRET, AUTH_GITHUB_SECRET, PLATFORM_ENCRYPTION_KEY, tenant llm_api_key, tenant docs_signer_secret, DATABASE_URL password); exact matches: none
Logs deleted before this run cannot be scanned; an exposure in them is outside this test.

results.claim: Dispatching a workflow cannot make it run anything but its own steps
results.method: zizmor template-injection audit (high confidence) of every workflow; dispatch inputs interpolated into run: blocks
results.summary: Dispatch inputs are expanded into shell scripts before any validation, so a caller able only to dispatch (GITHUB_PAT, or the actions:write GitHub App SECURITY.md recommends) can run code inside a job that holds id-token: write in the tenant's environment. That code can mint the tenant's cloud token and, on Azure, claim its application secrets. Passing inputs through env: and quoting them in the shell closes this.
evidence: deploy-tenant-azure.yml: 12 flagged steps; inputs deployment_id, tenant_id, tenant_slug, your_ecr_image, your_frontend_ecr_image; secrets in those steps PLATFORM_BASE_URL, PLATFORM_WEBHOOK_SECRET

results.claim: The deployment webhooks cannot be forged or replayed
results.method: Live requests to https://ai-chatbot-platform-gamma.vercel.app: near-miss webhook secrets, a replay against a finished deployment, and forged GitHub OIDC tokens; unit tests in src/app/api/deployments/[id]/status/route.test.ts and src/lib/deploymentSecrets.test.ts cover the same paths in-process
results.summary: 1 forged request(s) were refused by Vercel's firewall before reaching the platform, so they show the deployment is protected but do not exercise the platform's own check; src/lib/deploymentSecrets.test.ts covers those forgeries against the verifier directly.
